cls: Ergot derivative / alpha-adrenergic blocker (cerebral and peripheral vasodilator, nootropic)
pharm: A semisynthetic ergoline (ergot) derivative that blocks alpha-1 adrenoceptors causing vasodilatation and improved blood flow, while its nicotinic-acid moiety and other actions enhance cerebral metabolism and neurotransmission, giving combined vasoactive and nootropic effects used in cognitive and vascular disorders.

summary: Nicergoline is a semisynthetic ergot (ergoline) derivative used for symptomatic treatment of chronic cognitive and behavioural disorders of vascular or degenerative origin (such as age-related cognitive decline) and for peripheral and cerebral vascular disorders. It is a relatively selective alpha-1 adrenoceptor antagonist that produces vasodilatation and increases blood flow, and it also has metabolic (nootropic) effects enhancing cerebral glucose utilisation and neurotransmission. The typical dose is 30 mg twice daily (or 60 mg daily). The most common adverse effects relate to vasodilatation - orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, flushing and headache - and gastrointestinal upset. Because it is an ergot derivative, prolonged use carries the recognised ergot-class concerns of fibrotic reactions (pleural, retroperitoneal, cardiac valvular) and, rarely, ergotism; treatment benefit should be reviewed periodically. It can raise serum uric acid, so caution is needed in patients with gout or hyperuricaemia.
indications: Symptomatic treatment of chronic pathological cognitive and behavioural disorders of vascular or degenerative origin (e.g. age-related cognitive impairment, vascular dementia features)
Adjuvant treatment of acute and chronic peripheral and cerebral vascular (circulatory) disorders

dosage.n: Equivalent total of 60 mg/day; take at regular intervals

Reassess benefit periodically (e.g. after several months) and stop if no clear benefit

admin: Swallow tablets whole with water; take with or between meals
Take doses at evenly spaced intervals (e.g. morning and evening for twice-daily dosing)
Rise slowly from sitting or lying down, especially when starting, to reduce dizziness
Effect on cognitive symptoms develops gradually; review benefit after a few months
Report breathlessness, persistent cough, chest, abdominal or limb pain (possible fibrosis/ergotism)
moa: Nicergoline is an ergoline derivative whose main vascular action is selective antagonism of alpha-1 adrenoceptors, producing arterial and arteriolar vasodilatation and increasing cerebral and peripheral blood flow. In addition, its structure incorporates a nicotinic acid (bromo-nicotinate) moiety, and the drug exerts metabolic ('nootropic') effects: it enhances cerebral glucose uptake and utilisation, supports cholinergic and catecholaminergic neurotransmission, inhibits platelet aggregation, and may exert neurotrophic and antioxidant actions. The combination of improved perfusion and enhanced neuronal metabolism underlies its use in cognitive and vascular disorders. As an ergot derivative it can also interact with serotonergic and dopaminergic receptors, which is relevant to its fibrotic-reaction potential.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to nicergoline, other ergot alkaloids, or excipients
Pre-existing fibrotic disorders (pleural, pulmonary, retroperitoneal, cardiac valvular)
relative: Hyperuricaemia or history of gout (nicergoline can raise uric acid)
Concurrent treatment that lowers blood pressure or heart rate
Hyperprolactinaemia-related conditions / use of dopaminergic ergots
monitor: Blood pressure including orthostatic (lying and standing) measurements
Signs of fibrosis - dyspnoea, persistent cough, chest/abdominal/flank pain, oedema
Signs of ergotism - cold, painful or pale extremities, paraesthesia
Serum uric acid in those at risk of gout

preg: There are insufficient data on the use of nicergoline in pregnancy, and as an ergot derivative its safety has not been established. It is not recommended during pregnancy and should be used only if clearly necessary when no safer alternative exists.
lact: Nicergoline should be avoided during breastfeeding. Data on excretion in human milk are lacking, and ergot derivatives can inhibit lactation; use only if essential and consider discontinuing breastfeeding.
renal: In significant renal impairment the elimination of nicergoline and its metabolites may be reduced. The dose should be reduced and the patient monitored; caution is advised, and routine blood-pressure monitoring is recommended.
hepatic: Nicergoline is extensively metabolised in the liver. In hepatic impairment exposure may be increased; use a reduced dose with cautious titration and monitoring, and avoid in severe impairment unless clearly justified.

major: Other ergot alkaloids / ergot-derived agents - additive ergotism and fibrosis risk; avoid combination
Potent CYP2D6 inhibitors - may increase nicergoline metabolite exposure
moderate: Antihypertensives, alpha-blockers and other vasodilators - additive hypotension
Beta-blockers and other negative chronotropes - additive bradycardia / hypotension
Antiplatelet drugs and anticoagulants - nicergoline inhibits platelet aggregation; additive bleeding risk
Dopaminergic / serotonergic drugs - theoretical additive ergot-type receptor effects
minor: Drugs raising uric acid - additive hyperuricaemia
interactions.food: May be taken with or between meals; no clinically significant food interaction established.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol may add to the vasodilator and hypotensive effects, increasing dizziness; advise moderation.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor serum uric acid in at-risk patients; no specific characteristic laboratory interference.

serious: Fibrotic reactions - pleural, pulmonary, retroperitoneal or cardiac valvular fibrosis (prolonged use)
emergency: Signs of fibrosis (breathlessness, persistent cough, chest/abdominal/flank pain)

monitoring: Blood pressure including orthostatic measurements, especially at initiation
Periodic review of treatment benefit (avoid indefinite ergot exposure)
Signs and symptoms of fibrosis (respiratory, cardiac, abdominal) on long-term use
Signs of ergotism in the extremities
Serum uric acid in patients with gout or hyperuricaemia
counsel: Take the tablets as prescribed, usually twice a day with or between meals
Stand up slowly from sitting or lying down, especially when you first start, to avoid dizziness or fainting
It may take some weeks before any benefit on memory or circulation is noticeable
Tell your doctor if you develop shortness of breath, a lasting cough, or chest, tummy or back pain
Report cold, painful or pale fingers or toes
Limit alcohol, which can make dizziness worse, and do not stop the medicine without advice
pk: Vasoactive effect within hours; cognitive benefit develops over weeks
Plasma Tmax about 1-3 hours after oral dosing
Parent drug ~2-4 hours; active metabolites longer (allows once/twice-daily dosing)
Effect maintained with once- or twice-daily dosing
Store below 25-30 C, protect from light and moisture
pearls: NOT FDA-approved; this record is derived faithfully from EMA/SmPC and BNF sources, not from openFDA
Ergot derivative - prolonged use carries fibrosis risk (pleural, retroperitoneal, cardiac valvular); review benefit periodically and avoid in pre-existing fibrotic disease
Alpha-1 blockade causes orthostatic hypotension and dizziness - counsel patients to rise slowly
Can raise serum uric acid - use with caution in gout/hyperuricaemia
Combines vasodilator and metabolic (nootropic) actions; benefit on cognition is gradual and symptomatic
Avoid combining with other ergot alkaloids; watch additive bleeding risk with antiplatelets/anticoagulants
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your usual schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Overdose may cause marked but usually transient hypotension owing to alpha-blockade and vasodilatation. There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive: lay the patient supine with legs raised, give intravenous fluids, and monitor blood pressure and heart rate; vasopressor support (e.g. an agent acting on alpha receptors) may be required for severe, persistent hypotension. Treat other symptoms supportively and observe for signs of ergotism after very large ingestions.
